**Talking in the Dark**

The truest conversations happen in cars. Not because of the privacy — houses are private too — but because of the road. Two people side by side, both facing forward, the world arriving at sixty-five miles an hour and leaving just as fast. One of them watches the taillights, the other the long dark ribbon ahead, and neither watches the other, and that is exactly why the sentences come.

Eye contact is work. This is not a metaphor. It is a load on the mind, measurable in the lab. Show a child a hard question and the child's eyes leave yours and drift to the ceiling, the window, the middle distance, as if the answer were hiding there. In a sense it is. Looking away is how the brain makes room. Another person's face is not a neutral background; it is a presence to be read and managed, a second problem running underneath the first. Turn from it and the whole mind can go to the question. Turn toward it and some part of the mind is always spent on you.

So we have always built little machines for looking away. The confessional, with its screen and its dark, is one: the Church understood centuries before the psychologists that certain things cannot be said to a face. The campfire is another. For a hundred thousand years we sat with our faces to the flames and told each other what the day had hidden; the fire was the first television, a bright thing to look at together that is not each other, and maybe that is why stories exist. The letter is another. Give a person a page and no face at all and the pen will run to places the mouth would never dare. So are the radio call-in show, the late-night phone call, the haircut, the long walk with the dog, the shower. Freud put the patient on a couch for a reason: the analyst sits behind, unseen, a voice without a face, and the patient addresses the ceiling, which never judges and never blinks.

Even the taxi driver knows. People tell taxi drivers things they have not told their spouses. The driver is a professional non-watcher — eyes on the road, an occasional flick of the mirror, a back-of-the-head presence. The stranger on the night train, the stranger on the late flight: anyone whose face you will not have to see tomorrow is a priest.

And yet the gaze has its own genius, which is why we do not simply live in the dark. The look is how we check. It is slow, and it is for verification. When someone says *I love you* and needs to know it landed, they say *look at me.* When a parent needs to know whether the child is lying, they say *look at me.* The eyes are a test we give each other. Light is where we verify. Dark is where we produce. A face is for checking what has already been said. It is a poor place to say it.

This is why *we need to talk*, said across a kitchen table, is the worst sentence in a marriage, and why some of the best talks in a marriage happen on a walk, or in the car, or in bed with the lights off, both of you addressing the ceiling like a shared horizon.

Writing is the perfected form. It is talking in the dark with no face anywhere at all — not even a voice. That is its freedom and its danger. You can say anything; you cannot see the flinch. The page never looks back, which is why the page gets the truth, and why the truth on the page can be so hard to read aloud.

I am doing it now. No face, no eyes, a voice addressing a dark that may or may not be listening. It is the oldest comfortable posture we have: the fire, the road, the page. We say we want to bring things into the light. But the things that matter are said the way they have always been said — in the dark, in motion, to the flames, to the windshield, to no one, to the page.
